Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty Images NAZA Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’ ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence Sian Cain and agencies Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.54 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of NAZA , a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”. NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza that have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member. The 80-minute documentary won a special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. 0:50 NAZA director says ‘it’s important Israelis watch this film’ after win at Venice festival – video On Sunday Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors on X of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”. “I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X. Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank. ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence Read more “You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said on X. “I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.” The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied. In 2022 the supreme court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty”, for example by committing acts of espionage or treason. The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism”. The law requires the interior minister to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it. Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob after the world premiere of 2024’s No Other Land, which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank. “We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic,” he told the Guardian , adding: “For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons. “Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.” The Israeli military has responded to NAZA by saying it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary and criticised the use of anonymous testimonies, saying the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified”. The Palestinian militant group Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Hamas militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the subsequent three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties . – Agence France-Presse contributed to this report Explore more on these topics NAZA Israel Middle East and north Africa Gaza Palestine Israel-Gaza war news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Film Review ‘Winter of the Crow’: Dangerous Polaroids A naive professor sees the reality of communism when she attends a conference in Poland and takes Polaroids that put her in danger. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Professor Joan Andrews (Lesley Manville) in “Winter of the Crow.” Wild Mouse Productions Joe Bendel 10/8/2026 | Updated: 10/19/2026 0:00 X 1 NR | 1hr 52m | Drama, Thriller | 2026 Polaroids were the selfies of the 1980s, but they required film, so you could shoot only so many pictures with one cartridge. Professor Joan Andrews (Lesley Manville) happens to take a series of potentially explosive Polaroid photos during the first morning of martial law in 1981 Poland. The photos capture evidence of the murder of a Solidarity-aligned activist at the hands of the secret police. She also becomes a priority target in Kasia Adamik’s suspenseful “Winter of the Crow,” loosely adapted from Nobel Laureate Olga Tokarczuk’s short story “Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw.” Admittedly, Andrews is not very politically savvy, even by the standards of academic elites. Beyond the bitter cold of Poland’s winters, anyone following the news would understand that December 1981 was a less-than-ideal time to visit the communist nation. The regime was already arresting opposition leaders, especially members of the Solidarity democracy movement, while preparing to launch martial law on Dec. 13, 1981. Yet Andrews accepts an invitation to a psychology conference in Warsaw, without considering the political climate. Professor Joan Andrews (Lesley Manville), in “Winter of the Crow.” Wild Mouse Productions Then she is rather peeved when her speech (the night of Dec. 12) is interrupted by student protesters, led by Marek (Jakub Guszkowski); Marek likens life under communism to confinement in a mental asylum. Related Stories 24 Hours in Gdansk Pastor Artur Pawlowski Gets 60-Day Jail Sentence for Coutts Speech The professor will be further annoyed to discover that she must stay alone (with only a bottle of vodka) in a borrowed flat, instead of at the international hotel, because her hosts have no money. Consequently, she has no one to translate news of the new martial law edicts when she wakes the next morning. The tanks on the street are her first clue that something is amiss. Somehow, she evades the soldiers searching door-to-door for her student contact from the university, Alina Wachowiak (Zofia Wichlacz). Tragically, they find Wachowiak’s brother Marek instead. With her Polaroid camera, Andrews documents Marek’s death when police throw him out the window. However, by photographing Marek’s murder, she becomes the secret police’s most wanted fugitive. Fleeing on foot, Andrews tries to reach the only other contact Wachowiak gave her, Wachowiak’s uncle Henryk (Andrzej Konopka), who ardently supports Solidarity. It is definitely fair to ask what Andrews expected from communist Poland, but her obtuseness is sort of the point. Throughout “Winter of the Crow,” the spoiled academic must confront the life-and-death realities of communist oppression, which she never really considered before. Indeed, the film’s events constitute a rude awakening for Andrews. The British ambassador (Tom Burke) and professor Joan Andrews (Lesley Manville), in “Winter of the Crow.” Wild Mouse Productions Adamik also fittingly emphasizes the dystopian nature of communist Poland by envisioning Warsaw as a labyrinth of grim concrete housing projects and government office buildings. The immersive craftsmanship of the set and art design teams created an eerily effective period production. Every aspect of the city looks drably sinister, yet very much appropriate to the era. The film slyly uses the crows from Andrews’s nightmares as a striking visual motif and an allegory for the terror of martial law. As Wachowiak explains to her, the symbolism is aptly ironic because WRON, the Polish acronym for the new military junta under martial law, sounds similar to the Polish word for “crow.” Publicity still of director Kasia Adamik for “Winter of the Crow.” Gareth Cattermole. Getty Images Manhunt Thriller Despite Andrews’s flaws, “Winter of the Crow” successfully hooks the audience as a tense manhunt thriller. The professor’s ignorance further heightens the sense of jeopardy. Adamik often incorporates telling details that convey the tenor of those harsh times, such as when Andrews resorts to standing in ration lines for the collective body heat. Manville delivers a daring performance, fully embracing Andrews’s unsympathetic, unself-aware behavior throughout much of the film. Tanks are literally crushing dissent on the streets, yet she persists in seeing herself as the victim. Watching her slowly grasp the enormity of the events unfolding around her is exasperating, yet also strangely fascinating. The Polish supporting cast is first-rate, particularly Konopka, as the grizzled old Uncle Henryk. He embodies the working-class grit of the original Solidarity activists. Similarly, Wichlacz acutely captures the Polish people’s pain and frustration with life under communism. Tom Burke adds a touch of humor as the unnamed British ambassador, who might not be as befuddled as his civil service consular staff assumes. “Winter of the Crow” arrives at a timely moment. It shines a spotlight on the ruthlessness of totalitarian regimes and celebrates Solidarity’s courageous idealism. The bold imagery and taut atmosphere of paranoia really grab the audience’s attention. This is one of the better Cold War-era thrillers in some time, and an unusually thoughtfully rendered film. Highly recommended for intelligent audiences. “Winter of the Crow” releases in theaters Oct. 9. ‘Winter of the Crow’ Director: Kasia Adamik Starring: Lesley Manville, Zofia Wichlacz, Andrzej Konopka, Jakub Guszkowski, Tom Burke Not rated Running Time: 1 hour, 52 minutes Release Date: Oct. 9, 2026 Rated: 4 1/2 stars out of 5 What arts and culture topics would you like us to cover?
